findings.summary: The chapter's stakes were deleted: why the social credit question is the most dangerous one the book must answer, and why the reader who asks it is being responsible rather than paranoid.

evidence.baseline: There is a question that a significant fraction of thoughtful readers will arrive at, sooner or later, and it is the most dangerous question this book must answer, because if we do not answer it ourselves, our critics will answer it for us, and their answer will be fatal.
evidence.shipped: A reader may reasonably ask whether Providence is a biometric social credit system with gentler language.

findings.diagnosis: The shipped opener is clean and unafraid, but it deletes the argument for the chapter's existence: the critics-will-answer-first urgency, the concession that the resemblance is real enough that only a precise answer will do, and the promise of bright lines as design constraints rather than promises of good behavior. Those commitments are what the six lines are later held to. Restored in full.

evidence.baseline: The same fire that warms a house can burn it down. The question is never only what a technology can do, but what it is structurally forbidden from doing.
evidence.shipped: The same fire can warm a house or burn it. The design must specify what the instrument is forbidden to do.

openQuestions: The chapter heading. Why Providence Is Not Social Credit asserts the conclusion; The Bright Lines names the method. The restored chapter argues the first. Held under the structural hold, both forms recorded.

Impossibility language. The restored chapter says structurally forbidden, built to make impossible, and there is no database to seize, while the one credited keep in the Six Bright Lines child record says none of this should be called impossible to violate until the enforcement exists and has survived attack. Both stand unreconciled, deliberately, in the same pattern as the Stream Three incorruptible contradiction: the author's confidence and the pass's bound are both on the page for the author to reconcile.
The card anchor in F3, raised with the T-022 flag so one card revision can resolve both stranded anchors.
